nameStory: This beetle earned its "two-spotted" name from the pair of distinctive light-colored spots that stand out against its darker wing covers. The "handsome" part comes from the entire family name - these beetles were dubbed "handsome fungus beetles" because they're considered among the more attractive and well-proportioned of the fungus-eating beetle families.
description: The Two-spotted Handsome Fungus Beetle is a small, oval-shaped beetle that feeds on fungi growing on decaying wood. True to its name, it sports two pale yellowish or orange spots on its dark reddish-brown to black wing covers (called elytra). These compact beetles are typically around 4-6mm long - about the size of a small ladybug. Like other fungus beetles, they have a somewhat flattened, streamlined body that helps them navigate through the crevices of rotting logs and fungal growths.

idTips.label: Two pale spots
idTips.description: Look for two distinct yellowish or orange spots on the dark wing covers - these are the beetle's signature feature and are usually quite prominent against the darker background

idTips.label: Dark reddish-brown color
idTips.description: The body is typically dark reddish-brown to nearly black, with a smooth, somewhat glossy surface that feels hard and smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Small oval shape
idTips.description: About the size of your pinky nail, with a compact, oval body shape that's slightly flattened from top to bottom

idTips.label: Found on fungi
idTips.description: Almost always discovered crawling on or near bracket fungi, mushrooms, or fungal growths on decaying wood - they move slowly and deliberately

idTips.label: Clubbed antennae
idTips.description: The antennae are distinctly thicker at the tips, forming small clubs that help distinguish them from other small beetles

habitat: Look for these beetles in moist, shaded woodlands throughout New England, particularly in areas with plenty of decaying hardwood logs and stumps. They're most commonly found on or near bracket fungi, shelf fungi, and other wood-decomposing fungi in mixed and deciduous forests. You'll have the best luck searching in areas where fallen logs are beginning to soften and develop fungal growth.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under bark or in leaf litter. This is when they begin seeking out fresh fungal growth for feeding and reproduction.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily found crawling on fungi during warm, humid days. Look for them in early morning or evening when they're most active.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding on fungi while preparing for winter. They may be found clustering together under loose bark or in fungal crevices as they seek overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter hidden under bark, in rotting logs, or deep in leaf litter. They're essentially dormant and unlikely to be observed during cold months.

funFact: These beetles are actually performing an important ecological service - they help control harmful wood-decay fungi by eating them, acting like tiny forest janitors that help maintain the balance between beneficial and destructive fungal species in our woodlands.
confusionNotes: Small ladybugs are the most common mix-up, but remember that ladybugs are more dome-shaped and brightly colored, while handsome fungus beetles are flatter and darker with just two spots. Memory trick: "Handsome fungus beetles hang around fungi, ladybugs lunch on aphids."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "fungus beetles," these insects don't harm living trees - they only feed on fungi that grow on already dead or dying wood. This makes them beneficial forest inhabitants rather than pests, though their small size means they're often overlooked by casual observers.
compareHints: Since this is the only Endomychus species commonly found in New England, compare it with other handsome fungus beetles in different genera. Most other family members either lack the distinctive two-spot pattern or have different spot arrangements, making the Two-spotted relatively easy to identify once you know to look for fungi-associated beetles.
